title: Respiration — Krebs Cycle and Electron Transport System (Day 57)
introduction: This lesson details the biochemical steps that link glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation in plant mitochondria. Emphasis is on the link reaction, the Krebs (citric acid) cycle, and the electron transport system (ETS) with chemiosmotic ATP synthesis, all of which are high‑yield for NEET‑UG.

sections.heading: Link Reaction – Pyruvate Oxidation
sections.content: The link reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix where each pyruvate (3‑C) from glycolysis is decarboxylated, combined with CoA and reduced NAD⁺ to form acetyl‑CoA, CO₂ and NADH. The enzyme complex pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) catalyzes this irreversible step, linking glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
keyPoints: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl‑CoA + CO₂ + NADH
Irreversible, commits carbon to aerobic respiration
neetTips: Remember PDH is a multi‑enzyme complex – a common NEET factoid
Link reaction produces one NADH per pyruvate, i.e., two per glucose

sections.heading: Conversion of Pyruvate to Acetyl‑CoA
sections.content: During the link reaction, the 3‑carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂, and the remaining 2‑carbon fragment attaches to coenzyme A, forming acetyl‑CoA, the substrate that enters the Krebs cycle. This step also generates NADH, providing reducing equivalents for the ETS.
keyPoints: Produces NADH used later in ETS
neetTips: Link reaction is the only step that produces CO₂ before the Krebs cycle

sections.heading: Mitochondrial Matrix – Site of Central Metabolism
sections.content: The mitochondrial matrix is the innermost compartment bounded by the inner membrane. It houses the enzymes of the link reaction, the entire Krebs cycle, and the mitochondrial DNA. High concentrations of NAD⁺, FAD, ADP and inorganic phosphate reside here.
keyPoints: Contains enzymes of link reaction and Krebs cycle
Rich in NAD⁺, FAD, ADP, Pi
neetTips: All Krebs cycle reactions occur in the matrix – a frequent NEET diagram label

sections.heading: Krebs Cycle Overview
sections.content: Also called the citric acid cycle, it is a cyclic series of eight reactions that oxidize acetyl‑CoA to CO₂, while reducing NAD⁺ to NADH, FAD to FADH₂ and generating GTP/ATP. Each turn processes one acetyl‑CoA molecule.
keyPoints: Produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) per turn
neetTips: Remember the mnemonic: Citrate → Isocitrate → α‑KG → Succinyl‑CoA → Succinate → Fumarate → Malate → Oxaloacetate

sections.heading: Citric Acid Cycle – Detailed Sequence
sections.content: The cycle begins with condensation of acetyl‑CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate (citric acid). Subsequent isomerization, oxidative decarboxylations, substrate‑level phosphorylation and regeneration steps complete the cycle.
keyPoints: Citrate formation is the first step
Substrate‑level phosphorylation occurs at succinyl‑CoA synthetase
neetTips: Citrate → Isocitrate conversion is a simple rearrangement – often asked as a true/false

sections.heading: Oxaloacetic Acid – Cycle Starter and End‑Product
sections.content: Oxaloacetate (4‑C) condenses with acetyl‑CoA to form citrate, and is regenerated at the end of the cycle, ensuring continuity. It is derived from malate by oxidation via malate dehydrogenase.
keyPoints: Combines with acetyl‑CoA to start cycle
neetTips: Oxaloacetate is the only molecule that appears both at the start and end of the cycle

sections.heading: Citrate Formation – Condensation Reaction
sections.content: Acetyl‑CoA (2‑C) and oxaloacetate (4‑C) are combined by citrate synthase to produce citrate (6‑C) and CoA‑SH. This highly exergonic step drives the cycle forward.
neetTips: Citrate synthase reaction is the only irreversible step in the cycle

sections.heading: Decarboxylation Steps in the Krebs Cycle
sections.content: Two oxidative decarboxylations occur: (1) Isocitrate → α‑ketoglutarate (produces NADH and CO₂) catalyzed by isocitrate dehydrogenase; (2) α‑ketoglutarate → succinyl‑CoA (produces NADH and CO₂) catalyzed by α‑KG dehydrogenase complex.
keyPoints: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α‑KG dehydrogenase are NAD⁺‑dependent
neetTips: Both decarboxylation enzymes are regulated by NADH/NAD⁺ ratios – a common regulation question

sections.heading: NADH Generation in the Krebs Cycle
sections.content: Three NAD⁺ molecules are reduced to NADH per acetyl‑CoA: during isocitrate → α‑KG, α‑KG → succinyl‑CoA, and malate → oxaloacetate. NADH carries high‑energy electrons to the ETS.
neetTips: Count NADH: 3 per turn → 6 per glucose

sections.heading: FADH₂ Formation in the Krebs Cycle
sections.content: One molecule of FAD is reduced to FADH₂ during the conversion of succinate to fumarate, catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase, which is also part of Complex II of the ETS.
neetTips: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only Krebs enzyme embedded in the inner membrane

sections.heading: Substrate‑Level Phosphorylation – GTP/ATP Synthesis
sections.content: The conversion of succinyl‑CoA to succinate by succinyl‑CoA synthetase generates GTP (or ATP in some tissues) directly via substrate‑level phosphorylation, independent of the ETS.
keyPoints: One GTP (or ATP) per cycle turn
neetTips: GTP can be readily converted to ATP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase

sections.heading: Regeneration of Oxaloacetate – Cycle Completion
sections.content: Malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate by malate dehydrogenase, producing the final NADH and restoring the 4‑C acceptor for the next acetyl‑CoA molecule.
neetTips: The NADH from this step is often the last NADH counted in the cycle

sections.heading: Electron Transport System (ETS) Overview
sections.content: The ETS comprises four inner‑membrane protein complexes (I–IV) and mobile carriers (ubiquinone and cytochrome c). Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ travel through these complexes, releasing energy used to pump protons into the intermembrane space.
keyPoints: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) receives electrons from NADH
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) receives electrons from FADH₂
Ubiquinone and cytochrome c shuttle electrons
Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O
neetTips: Remember the order: NADH → I → Q → III → cytochrome c → IV

sections.heading: Inner Mitochondrial Membrane – Functional Barrier
sections.content: The inner membrane is highly impermeable, housing the ETS complexes and ATP synthase. Its folded cristae increase surface area, maximizing proton pumping and ATP synthesis.
keyPoints: Contains ETS complexes I‑IV, ATP synthase
neetTips: Proton gradient is established across this membrane, not the outer membrane

sections.heading: Mobile Electron Carriers – Ubiquinone and Cytochrome c
sections.content: Ubiquinone (CoQ) accepts electrons from Complex I and II, becoming ubiquinol, and transfers them to Complex III. Cytochrome c shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV. Both are essential for electron flow.
keyPoints: Ubiquinone (Q) ↔ ubiquinol (QH₂) between I/II and III
Cytochrome c transfers electrons from III to IV
neetTips: Both carriers are soluble in the inner membrane lipid bilayer, facilitating rapid electron transfer

sections.heading: Proton Gradient – Chemiosmotic Driving Force
sections.content: As electrons move through Complexes I, III and IV, protons are pumped from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical gradient (ΔpH + membrane potential) that stores potential energy.
keyPoints: Protons pumped at Complex I, III, IV
Creates both ΔpH and electrical potential
neetTips: The gradient is the basis of chemiosmosis – a classic NEET diagram

sections.heading: Chemiosmosis – Coupling Gradient to ATP Synthesis
sections.content: Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase (Complex V), driving rotation of its γ‑subunit and catalyzing the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. This process is termed oxidative phosphorylation.
keyPoints: Proton flow through ATP synthase provides energy
Rotational mechanism converts ADP + Pi → ATP
neetTips: Remember P/O ratio: ~2.5 ATP per NADH, ~1.5 per FADH₂

sections.heading: ATP Synthase Structure and Function
sections.content: ATP synthase consists of F₀ (membrane‑embedded proton channel) and F₁ (catalytic) domains. Proton movement through F₀ causes conformational changes in F₁, synthesizing ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
neetTips: ATP synthase is sometimes called the 'molecular turbine'

sections.heading: Oxidative Phosphorylation – Final ATP Yield
sections.content: The combined action of the ETS and chemiosmosis is called oxidative phosphorylation. Approximately 34‑36 ATP molecules are generated per glucose molecule when oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor.
neetTips: Add 2 ATP from glycolysis and 2 from link reaction to get total ~38 in prokaryotes; plants have slightly lower due to transport costs

sections.heading: Oxygen – Terminal Electron Acceptor
sections.content: Molecular oxygen (O₂) accepts electrons at Complex IV, combining with protons to form water. This step maintains electron flow and prevents backup of the ETS.
neetTips: Absence of O₂ halts ETS → lactic acid fermentation

sections.heading: Water Formation in the ETS
sections.content: The four electrons transferred to O₂ at Complex IV combine with four protons from the matrix to produce two molecules of H₂O, completing the respiratory chain.
neetTips: Water formation is the ultimate fate of electrons from NADH/FADH₂

sections.heading: Respiratory Quotient (RQ) Overview
sections.content: RQ = CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed. For carbohydrate oxidation (glucose) RQ ≈ 1.0, reflecting equal moles of CO₂ and O₂. Fat oxidation yields RQ ≈ 0.7, protein ≈ 0.8. RQ helps infer substrate utilization.
neetTips: NEET often asks RQ value for glucose – answer 1.0

learningOutcome: Explain the link reaction and formation of acetyl‑CoA
Describe each step, intermediates and energy yield of the Krebs (citric acid) cycle
Illustrate the components and operation of the electron transport system and chemiosmotic ATP synthesis
Interpret the respiratory quotient and its significance for substrate metabolism

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the site of the link reaction in eukaryotic cells?
mcqs.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA in the mitochondrial matrix.

mcqs.question: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) requires all of the following co‑enzymes EXCEPT:
mcqs.explanation: Biotin is a co‑enzyme for carboxylation reactions (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase) but not for the PDC; the required co‑enzymes are TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+.

mcqs.question: During the link reaction, one molecule of pyruvate yields which of the following products?
mcqs.explanation: One pyruvate is decarboxylated to release one CO₂, and the remaining two‑carbon fragment is transferred to CoA, producing acetyl‑CoA and one NADH.

mcqs.question: Which regulatory mechanism directly inhibits the activity of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
options: High levels of acetyl‑CoA and NADH
High levels of ADP and inorganic phosphate
mcqs.explanation: Acetyl‑CoA and NADH are allosteric inhibitors of PDC, signalling that the cell already has sufficient energy and building blocks.

mcqs.question: In the link reaction, the carbon atom that is released as CO₂ originates from which carbon of pyruvate?
options: All three carbons are equally likely
mcqs.explanation: The carboxyl carbon (C‑1) of pyruvate is removed as CO₂ during the decarboxylation step catalyzed by the E1 component of PDC.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best explains why the link reaction is considered irreversible under cellular conditions?
options: It involves a highly exergonic decarboxylation coupled with NAD⁺ reduction
It requires ATP hydrolysis to proceed
It is driven by substrate-level phosphorylation
It is reversible but the equilibrium lies far to the left
mcqs.explanation: The decarboxylation of pyruvate and the reduction of NAD⁺ to NADH release a large amount of free energy, making the overall reaction essentially irreversible.

mcqs.question: A deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B₁) would most directly affect which step of the link reaction?
options: Transfer of the acetyl group to CoA
mcqs.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the co‑enzyme of the E1 component that catalyses the decarboxylation of pyruvate; its deficiency impairs this step.

mcqs.question: Where does the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA take place in the cell?
mcqs.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is located in the mitochondrial matrix, where pyruvate is oxidatively decarboxylated to acetyl‑CoA.

mcqs.question: During the link reaction, which coenzyme is reduced?
mcqs.explanation: NAD+ accepts the electrons released in the oxidation of pyruvate and is reduced to NADH.

mcqs.question: The decarboxylation step catalyzed by the E1 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires which vitamin‑derived cofactor?
mcqs.explanation: E1 (pyruvate dehydrogenase) uses thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor to remove the carboxyl group from pyruvate.

mcqs.question: One molecule of pyruvate yields how many molecules of NADH in the conversion to acetyl‑CoA?
mcqs.explanation: The oxidative decarboxylation of one pyruvate produces one NADH molecule.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) is FALSE?
mcqs.explanation: Phosphorylation of the PDC by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase inactivates, not activates, the complex.

mcqs.question: The lipoic acid cofactor is covalently attached to which subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
mcqs.explanation: Lipoic acid is bound to the E2 subunit, where it swings intermediates between active sites.

mcqs.question: In acetyl‑CoA formed from pyruvate, the two carbon atoms originate from which parts of the original pyruvate molecule?
options: Both the carbonyl (C2) and methyl (C3) carbons
mcqs.explanation: During decarboxylation, the carboxyl carbon (C1) is released as CO2; the remaining carbonyl (C2) and methyl (C3) carbons become the acetyl group of acetyl‑CoA.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme of the citric acid cycle is located in the mitochondrial matrix?
mcqs.explanation: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the Krebs cycle and is situated in the mitochondrial matrix, whereas the other listed proteins are components of the inner membrane electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: The mitochondrial matrix provides the site for which of the following reactions?
options: Proton pumping across the inner membrane
mcqs.explanation: Pyruvate is imported into the matrix where the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts it to acetyl‑CoA; the other processes occur in the inner membrane.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the mitochondrial matrix is FALSE?
options: It contains all the enzymes of the Krebs cycle
It is the site of oxidative phosphorylation
It has a high concentration of NAD+ and NADH
It is bounded by the inner mitochondrial membrane
mcqs.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not in the matrix; the matrix houses the Krebs‑cycle enzymes and the NAD+/NADH pool.

mcqs.question: Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA occurs in which mitochondrial compartment?
mcqs.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex resides in the matrix, where it decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA.

mcqs.question: Which ion has a markedly higher concentration in the mitochondrial matrix than in the cytosol?
mcqs.explanation: The matrix accumulates Ca2+ ions, which regulate several matrix enzymes; H+ concentration is low in the matrix relative to the intermembrane space.

mcqs.question: Why can NADH generated in the mitochondrial matrix not directly donate electrons to the electron transport chain?
options: NADH cannot cross the inner membrane
The inner membrane is impermeable to NADH
NADH is used for ATP synthesis in the matrix
mcqs.explanation: The inner mitochondrial membrane does not allow NADH to pass; instead, its electrons are transferred to the chain via shuttle systems (e.g., malate‑aspartate shuttle).

mcqs.question: Which metabolite is NOT normally present in the mitochondrial matrix during aerobic respiration?
mcqs.explanation: Cytochrome c is a peripheral protein of the inner membrane facing the intermembrane space, whereas oxaloacetate, succinate and malate are intermediates of the Krebs cycle in the matrix.

mcqs.question: Where does the Krebs cycle take place in eukaryotic cells?
mcqs.explanation: All the enzymes of the citric acid cycle are soluble and function in the mitochondrial matrix, the innermost compartment of mitochondria.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the isomerization of citrate to isocitrate?
mcqs.explanation: Aconitase removes a water molecule from citrate to form cis‑aconitate and then adds water to produce isocitrate.

mcqs.question: How many molecules of NADH are produced per one acetyl‑CoA that enters the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: NADH is generated in three oxidative steps: isocitrate → α‑KG, α‑KG → succinyl‑CoA, and malate → oxaloacetate.

mcqs.question: Which step of the Krebs cycle directly yields GTP (or ATP) by substrate‑level phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: Succinyl‑CoA synthetase converts succinyl‑CoA to succinate, coupling the reaction to the formation of GTP (or ATP in some organisms).

mcqs.question: The oxidative decarboxylation of α‑ketoglutarate to succinyl‑CoA is analogous to which other Krebs‑cycle reaction?
mcqs.explanation: Both isocitrate → α‑KG and α‑KG → succinyl‑CoA involve NAD⁺‑dependent oxidative decarboxylation, releasing CO₂ and producing NADH.

mcqs.question: Which of the following compounds is NOT an intermediate of the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Pyruvate is converted to acetyl‑CoA before entering the cycle; it does not appear as a cycle intermediate.

mcqs.question: Approximately how many ATP equivalents are generated from one turn of the Krebs cycle, including oxidative phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: One turn yields 3 NADH (3 × 2.5 = 7.5 ATP), 1 FADH₂ (1 × 1.5 = 1.5 ATP), and 1 GTP (≈1 ATP), totaling about 10 ATP equivalents.

mcqs.question: In the step catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase, which coenzyme is reduced and where is the enzyme located?
options: FAD in the inner mitochondrial membrane
mcqs.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) reduces FAD to FADH₂ and is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, linking the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the reversible conversion of citrate to isocitrate in the citric acid cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Aconitase catalyzes the dehydration of citrate to cis‑aconitate followed by hydration to form isocitrate.

mcqs.question: The decarboxylation step that yields CO₂ and NADH during the citric acid cycle is carried out by which enzyme?
mcqs.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate, producing CO₂ and NADH.

mcqs.question: How many molecules of GTP (or ATP) are generated directly by substrate‑level phosphorylation in one complete turn of the citric acid cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Succinyl‑CoA synthetase converts succinyl‑CoA to succinate, generating one molecule of GTP (or ATP) per cycle turn.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a product of one turn of the citric acid cycle?
mcqs.explanation: The cycle produces NADH, FADH₂, CO₂ and GTP, but no NADPH is formed.

mcqs.question: The conversion of α‑ketoglutarate to succinyl‑CoA in the citric acid cycle yields which reduced cofactor?
mcqs.explanation: α‑Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes this step and reduces NAD⁺ to NADH.

mcqs.question: In which mitochondrial compartment does the citric acid cycle take place?
mcqs.explanation: All the enzymes of the citric acid cycle are located in the mitochondrial matrix.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly describes a regulatory feature of the citric acid cycle?
options: Citrate synthase is allosterically activated by ATP
Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by NADH
α‑Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP
Succinate dehydrogenase is inhibited by O₂
mcqs.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is allosterically inhibited by high NADH (and ATP), reducing cycle flux when energy is abundant.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly describes the role of oxaloacetic acid in the Krebs cycle?
options: It combines with acetyl‑CoA to form citrate
It is decarboxylated to form α‑ketoglutarate
It donates electrons directly to the electron transport chain
mcqs.explanation: Oxaloacetate condenses with acetyl‑CoA, catalyzed by citrate synthase, to produce citrate, the first step of the cycle.

mcqs.question: The enzyme that synthesizes oxaloacetate from pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix is:
mcqs.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase catalyzes the ATP‑dependent carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, an anaplerotic reaction.

mcqs.question: Oxaloacetate is regenerated in the Krebs cycle by which specific reaction?
options: Oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate by malate dehydrogenase
mcqs.explanation: Malate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate, completing the cycle.

mcqs.question: In mitochondrial anaplerotic pathways, oxaloacetate can be formed directly from which substrate?
mcqs.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, replenishing cycle intermediates.

mcqs.question: Under prolonged fasting, the mitochondrial concentration of oxaloacetate:
options: Remains unchanged due to rapid turnover
Increases because pyruvate carboxylase activity is up‑regulated
Is exported to the cytosol for gluconeogenesis
mcqs.explanation: Fasting stimulates gluconeogenesis; pyruvate carboxylase activity rises, producing more oxaloacetate to serve both the cycle and gluconeogenic flux.

mcqs.question: Which molecular formula corresponds to oxaloacetic acid?
mcqs.explanation: Oxaloacetic acid contains four carbon atoms, four hydrogen atoms, and five oxygen atoms, giving the formula C4H4O5.

mcqs.question: The condensation of acetyl‑CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate is catalyzed by which enzyme, and what is the immediate product?
mcqs.explanation: Citrate synthase catalyzes the condensation of acetyl‑CoA and oxaloacetate, yielding citrate as the first Krebs‑cycle intermediate.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the condensation of acetyl‑CoA and oxaloacetate to form citrate in the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the Krebs cycle, combining acetyl‑CoA with oxaloacetate to produce citrate and CoA.

mcqs.question: In which cellular compartment does citrate formation occur during aerobic respiration?
mcqs.explanation: All reactions of the Krebs cycle, including citrate formation, take place in the mitochondrial matrix.

mcqs.question: The condensation of acetyl‑CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate results in the release of which molecule?
mcqs.explanation: During the citrate synthase reaction, the thioester bond of acetyl‑CoA is cleaved, releasing free CoA‑SH.

mcqs.question: How many carbon atoms in citrate are contributed by acetyl‑CoA and how many by oxaloacetate?
mcqs.explanation: Acetyl‑CoA provides a two‑carbon acetyl group, while oxaloacetate contributes four carbons, giving the six‑carbon citrate molecule.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the citrate synthase reaction is correct?
options: It is an irreversible, highly exergonic step of the Krebs cycle
It requires direct ATP hydrolysis to proceed
It is a reversible equilibrium that can readily run in both directions
It is activated by high concentrations of NADH
mcqs.explanation: The citrate synthase reaction has a large negative ΔG°, making it essentially irreversible under cellular conditions.

mcqs.question: Which metabolite acts as an allosteric inhibitor of citrate synthase, thereby regulating the entry of acetyl‑CoA into the cycle?
mcqs.explanation: High cellular ATP levels signal sufficient energy and inhibit citrate synthase, slowing the Krebs cycle.

mcqs.question: The chemical mechanism of citrate formation involves which type of reaction?
mcqs.explanation: Oxaloacetate attacks the carbonyl carbon of the acetyl‑CoA thioester in a nucleophilic acyl substitution, forming citrate and releasing CoA.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA in the mitochondrial matrix?
mcqs.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) performs oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, producing acetyl‑CoA, CO₂ and NADH.

mcqs.question: In the Krebs cycle, which step involves a decarboxylation that also generates NADH and CO₂?
mcqs.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate, producing NADH and releasing CO₂.

mcqs.question: The decarboxylation of α‑ketoglutarate to succinyl‑CoA is analogous to the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction because both require which cofactor?
mcqs.explanation: Both reactions are oxidative decarboxylations that need Coenzyme A to accept the acyl group, forming acetyl‑CoA or succinyl‑CoA.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about decarboxylation reactions in the Krebs cycle is FALSE?
options: They are irreversible under cellular conditions
They are coupled to NAD⁺ reduction
mcqs.explanation: Decarboxylation steps do not directly produce ATP; ATP (or GTP) is generated later by substrate‑level phosphorylation or oxidative phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: During the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, the carbon released as CO₂ originates from which carbon of glucose?
mcqs.explanation: The carboxyl carbon of pyruvate (C‑1 of pyruvate) comes from carbon‑3 of glucose after glycolysis, and this carbon is released as CO₂ in the PDH reaction.

mcqs.question: Which molecule acts as the primary electron acceptor in the oxidative decarboxylation steps of the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Both pyruvate dehydrogenase and the two dehydrogenases of the cycle reduce NAD⁺ to NADH while decarboxylating their substrates.

mcqs.question: The decarboxylation of isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate by isocitrate dehydrogenase requires which metal ion as a cofactor?
mcqs.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a Mg²⁺ (or Mn²⁺) dependent enzyme; the metal ion assists in substrate binding and catalysis.

mcqs.question: How many molecules of NADH are generated from the conversion of one molecule of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA in the mitochondrial matrix?
mcqs.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, producing one NADH per pyruvate molecule.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme‑catalyzed step of the citric acid cycle yields NADH by oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate?
mcqs.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase converts isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate, reducing NAD⁺ to NADH in the process.

mcqs.question: In one complete turn of the Krebs cycle, how many NADH molecules are produced?
mcqs.explanation: Three dehydrogenase reactions (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase) each generate one NADH, totaling three per cycle.

mcqs.question: The NADH generated in the mitochondrial matrix donates its electrons to which complex of the electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: NADH transfers its electrons to Complex I, also called NADH dehydrogenase, initiating the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about NADH production during the Krebs cycle is FALSE?
options: NADH is generated during the conversion of malate to oxaloacetate.
NADH is generated during the conversion of succinate to fumarate.
NADH is generated during the conversion of isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate.
NADH is generated during the conversion of α‑ketoglutarate to succinyl‑CoA.
mcqs.explanation: The succinate → fumarate step is catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase and produces FADH₂, not NADH.

mcqs.question: Considering the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule, how many NADH molecules are produced from pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle (excluding glycolysis)?
mcqs.explanation: Each glucose yields 2 pyruvate → 2 NADH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) and 2 turns of the Krebs cycle → 6 NADH, giving a total of 8 NADH.

mcqs.question: The production of NADH in the step catalyzed by α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is coupled with which of the following processes?
mcqs.explanation: α‑Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyzes a decarboxylation reaction that reduces NAD⁺ to NADH while releasing CO₂.

mcqs.question: Which step of the Krebs cycle results in the formation of FADH2?
mcqs.explanation: The succinate dehydrogenase-catalyzed oxidation of succinate to fumarate reduces FAD to FADH2, producing one FADH2 per cycle.

mcqs.question: In plant mitochondria, the enzyme that generates FADH2 during the Krebs cycle is a component of which electron transport chain complex?
mcqs.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase, which produces FADH2, is embedded in the inner membrane as Complex II of the ETC.

mcqs.question: One molecule of FADH2 formed in the Krebs cycle yields approximately how many ATP equivalents via oxidative phosphorylation in plant cells?
mcqs.explanation: Electrons from FADH2 enter the ETC at Complex II, bypassing Complex I, and generate about 1.5 ATP per FADH2 under typical P/O ratios.

mcqs.question: During the conversion of succinate to fumarate, which cofactor directly accepts the electrons?
mcqs.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase uses flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as the electron acceptor, producing FADH2.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the FADH2 produced in the Krebs cycle is FALSE?
options: It donates electrons to ubiquinone (CoQ) in the ETC.
It is generated in the mitochondrial matrix.
It enters the ETC at Complex I.
Its oxidation contributes to the proton gradient across the inner membrane.
mcqs.explanation: FADH2 does not enter the ETC at Complex I; it transfers electrons to ubiquinone at Complex II, bypassing Complex I.

mcqs.question: What is the net number of FADH2 molecules produced per molecule of glucose oxidized in plant cells?
mcqs.explanation: Each glucose yields two acetyl‑CoA molecules; each turn of the cycle produces one FADH2, giving a total of two FADH2 per glucose.

mcqs.question: If a plant cell is treated with malonate, a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, what immediate effect on FADH2 production will occur?
mcqs.explanation: Malonate blocks succinate dehydrogenase, preventing the succinate → fumarate step and thus reducing the production of FADH2.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the substrate‑level phosphorylation that generates GTP during the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Succinyl‑CoA synthetase converts succinyl‑CoA to succinate, coupling the conversion of GDP + Pi to GTP, which is a classic substrate‑level phosphorylation step in the cycle.

mcqs.question: In one complete turn of the Krebs cycle, how many molecules of ATP (or its equivalent) are produced directly by substrate‑level phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: Only the succinyl‑CoA synthetase step yields GTP (equivalent to one ATP) per cycle; all other high‑energy molecules are generated later by oxidative phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: The GTP formed in the Krebs cycle can be readily converted to ATP by which enzyme?
mcqs.explanation: Nucleoside diphosphate kinase catalyzes the reversible transfer of the terminal phosphate from GTP to ADP, forming ATP and GDP.

mcqs.question: Where does the ATP synthesis driven by the proton motive force occur during oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Matrix side of inner mitochondrial membrane
mcqs.explanation: ATP synthase (Complex V) is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane with its catalytic domain facing the matrix, where ADP and Pi are phosphorylated to ATP.

mcqs.question: Approximately how many molecules of ATP are generated per NADH oxidized in the electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: Current bioenergetic estimates assign about 2.5 ATP molecules to each NADH oxidized, reflecting the proton translocation stoichiometry of Complexes I, III and IV.

mcqs.question: Which molecule donates electrons directly to Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: Complex I receives electrons from NADH, which are then passed through a series of carriers to ubiquinone, contributing to the proton gradient.

mcqs.question: The conversion of succinyl‑CoA to succinate in the Krebs cycle results in GTP formation. This step is an example of:
options: Generation of a proton gradient across the inner membrane
mcqs.explanation: GTP is produced directly by transferring a phosphate from inorganic phosphate to GDP, without involvement of the electron transport chain, classifying it as substrate‑level phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the final step of oxaloacetate regeneration in the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate to oxaloacetate, completing the regeneration of oxaloacetate in the cycle.

mcqs.question: The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, an anaplerotic reaction, is catalysed by which mitochondrial enzyme and requires which cofactor?
mcqs.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase, a biotin‑dependent enzyme, carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate, replenishing the cycle.

mcqs.question: Which molecule allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase, enhancing oxaloacetate regeneration?
mcqs.explanation: Acetyl‑CoA binds to pyruvate carboxylase and increases its activity, linking acetyl‑CoA availability to oxaloacetate formation.

mcqs.question: During the regeneration of oxaloacetate, malate is oxidised to oxaloacetate producing which reduced coenzyme?
mcqs.explanation: Malate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from malate to NAD+, forming NADH.

mcqs.question: Which statement about oxaloacetate regeneration in the Krebs cycle is true?
options: It is catalysed by a reversible reaction
mcqs.explanation: The malate‑oxaloacetate interconversion catalysed by malate dehydrogenase is reversible and depends on the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

mcqs.question: A high mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio will shift the malate dehydrogenase reaction in which direction?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated NADH drives the reaction toward malate, reducing oxaloacetate regeneration.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a pathway that directly replenishes oxaloacetate for the Krebs cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Succinate to fumarate is a step within the cycle and does not generate oxaloacetate; the other three provide oxaloacetate or its precursors.

mcqs.question: Which complex of the mitochondrial electron transport chain directly transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone?
mcqs.explanation: Complex I oxidises NADH and passes the electrons to ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), initiating the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: The immediate electron donor to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is:
mcqs.explanation: Reduced cytochrome c carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV, where they are finally transferred to oxygen.

mcqs.question: Which of the following complexes does NOT contribute to proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
mcqs.explanation: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons to ubiquinone but does not translocate protons across the membrane.

mcqs.question: The approximate P/O ratio (ATP molecules formed per atom of oxygen reduced) for NADH oxidation in mitochondria is:
mcqs.explanation: Oxidation of one NADH typically yields about 2.5–3 ATP; NEET textbooks often quote a value of 3 as the P/O ratio.

mcqs.question: Which inhibitor blocks electron flow from ubiquinol to cytochrome c?
mcqs.explanation: Antimycin A binds to Complex III and prevents transfer of electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c.

mcqs.question: According to the chemiosmotic theory, ATP synthesis in oxidative phosphorylation is driven by:
options: Direct transfer of electrons to ADP
Flow of protons back into the matrix through ATP synthase
Movement of electrons through Complex IV
mcqs.explanation: The proton motive force generated by electron transport drives protons back into the matrix via ATP synthase, coupling this flow to ATP formation.

mcqs.question: The final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain is:
mcqs.explanation: Molecular oxygen accepts the electrons at Complex IV, being reduced to water, completing the chain.

mcqs.question: Which lipid is uniquely abundant in the inner mitochondrial membrane and essential for the activity of several electron transport chain complexes?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiolipin, a diphosphatidylglycerol, is enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane and stabilizes complexes I, III and IV, facilitating efficient electron transport.

mcqs.question: The inner mitochondrial membrane is essentially impermeable to which ion, necessitating specific transport proteins for its movement?
mcqs.explanation: Protons cannot cross the inner membrane freely; their controlled movement through complexes I, III, IV and ATP synthase creates the proton motive force required for ATP synthesis.

mcqs.question: The proton motive force generated across the inner mitochondrial membrane is harnessed by which enzyme complex to produce ATP?
mcqs.explanation: ATP synthase (Complex V) uses the flow of protons back into the matrix through its F₀ subunit to drive phosphorylation of ADP to ATP in the F₁ subunit.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about the inner mitochondrial membrane is FALSE?
options: It contains the enzymes of the citric acid cycle
It houses the electron transport chain complexes
It is highly folded forming cristae
It is relatively impermeable to ions
mcqs.explanation: All enzymes of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle are located in the mitochondrial matrix, not in the inner membrane.

mcqs.question: The primary site where oxidative phosphorylation occurs is:
mcqs.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation involves the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, both embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

mcqs.question: Which carrier protein transports ADP into the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane in exchange for ATP?
mcqs.explanation: The adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT) exchanges matrix ADP for cytosolic ATP, maintaining the supply of ADP for phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: Approximately what percentage of the inner mitochondrial membrane’s mass is protein, reflecting its high protein‑to‑lipid ratio?
mcqs.explanation: The inner mitochondrial membrane is about 70% protein by weight, a much higher proportion than most other cellular membranes, due to the dense packing of respiratory complexes.

mcqs.question: Which molecule is the primary electron donor that transfers electrons to Complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: NADH generated in the mitochondrial matrix donates its two electrons to Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), initiating the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: Ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q) primarily functions as:
options: A mobile lipid‑soluble electron carrier within the inner mitochondrial membrane
A fixed protein component of Complex II
A proton pump that directly translocates H+ across the membrane
The terminal electron acceptor that reduces O2
mcqs.explanation: Coenzyme Q is a small, lipid‑soluble molecule that shuttles electrons between Complexes I/II and Complex III while diffusing laterally in the inner membrane.

mcqs.question: Which electron carrier transfers electrons from Complex III to Complex IV in the mitochondrial ETC?
mcqs.explanation: Cytochrome c is a small, water‑soluble heme protein that moves electrons from the cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III) to cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV).

mcqs.question: The reduced form of coenzyme Q is called:
mcqs.explanation: When coenzyme Q accepts two electrons and two protons, it becomes ubiquinol (QH2), the reduced, electron‑rich form.

mcqs.question: Which electron carrier has the most negative standard reduction potential, making it the best electron donor in the ETC?
mcqs.explanation: The NAD⁺/NADH couple has a standard reduction potential of about –0.32 V, more negative than FAD/FADH₂ (–0.22 V) and ubiquinone (–0.045 V), so NADH is the strongest donor.

mcqs.question: Which statement is FALSE regarding electron carriers in the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
options: Cytochrome c is a water‑soluble protein that diffuses in the intermembrane space
Ubiquinone can accept and donate two electrons at a time
NADH transfers electrons directly to Complex IV
FADH₂ enters the chain at Complex II
mcqs.explanation: NADH does not transfer electrons directly to Complex IV; it first donates them to Complex I, which then passes them through the chain to Complex IV.

mcqs.question: One molecule of ubiquinone (Q) can transport how many electrons during a single turn of the electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: Ubiquinone can accept two electrons (and two protons) to become ubiquinol, allowing it to carry a pair of electrons from Complex I or II to Complex III.

mcqs.question: Which mitochondrial electron transport chain complex does NOT contribute to the formation of the proton gradient by pumping protons across the inner membrane?
mcqs.explanation: Complex II transfers electrons from succinate to ubiquinone but does not pump protons, whereas Complexes I, III and IV actively translocate protons to generate the gradient.

mcqs.question: The proton motive force that drives ATP synthesis consists of which two components?
mcqs.explanation: The proton motive force (pmf) is the sum of the chemical gradient (ΔpH) and the electrical gradient (Δψ) across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

mcqs.question: Approximately how many protons must re-enter the mitochondrial matrix through ATP synthase to synthesize one molecule of ATP (including the transport of ADP and Pi) in mammalian mitochondria?
mcqs.explanation: Experimental data indicate that about 4 protons are required per ATP synthesized in mammalian mitochondria (3 for the rotary mechanism and 1 for ADP/Pi transport).

mcqs.question: When an uncoupling agent such as dinitrophenol collapses the proton gradient, what is the immediate effect on the rate of oxygen consumption by isolated mitochondria?
mcqs.explanation: By dissipating the gradient, uncouplers stimulate the electron transport chain to work faster in an attempt to re‑establish the gradient, leading to an increased rate of O₂ consumption.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the proton gradient generated during oxidative phosphorylation is FALSE?
options: It is generated by complexes that pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space
The gradient is used solely for ATP synthesis
The gradient contributes to the membrane potential
mcqs.explanation: Besides ATP synthesis, the proton gradient also drives the import of metabolites (e.g., phosphate, ADP) and the export of citrate; therefore it is not used solely for ATP production.

mcqs.question: Oxidation of one molecule of NADH releases about –220 kJ mol⁻¹. Roughly how much of this energy is conserved in the synthesis of ATP (assuming 3 ATP are formed per NADH)?
mcqs.explanation: Each ATP synthesis requires ~30 kJ mol⁻¹; three ATP therefore store about 90 kJ, which is the fraction of the total energy conserved.

mcqs.question: In mitochondria, protons flow down their electrochemical gradient to drive ATP synthesis. From which compartment do they move?
options: From the matrix to the intermembrane space
From the intermembrane space to the matrix
From the cytosol to the matrix
From the matrix to the cytosol
mcqs.explanation: The proton gradient has a higher proton concentration in the intermembrane space; protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, providing the energy for phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: According to the chemiosmotic mechanism, ATP synthesis in mitochondria is driven by
options: direct transfer of electrons to ADP
the flow of protons back into the matrix through ATP synthase
oxidation of NADH by complex II
mcqs.explanation: ATP synthase utilizes the energy released when protons move down their electrochemical gradient from the intermembrane space into the matrix, converting ADP + Pi into ATP.

mcqs.question: Which component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain does NOT pump protons across the inner membrane?
mcqs.explanation: Complex II transfers electrons from succinate to ubiquinone but does not translocate protons; the other three complexes contribute to the proton gradient.

mcqs.question: In chemiosmotic oxidative phosphorylation, the final electron acceptor that combines with protons to form a stable product is
mcqs.explanation: Molecular oxygen accepts electrons at complex IV and combines with protons to produce water, completing the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: The approximate P/O ratio (inorganic phosphate per atom of oxygen reduced) for the oxidation of one molecule of NADH in mitochondria is
mcqs.explanation: Oxidation of NADH typically yields about 3 molecules of ATP, giving a P/O ratio close to 3.

mcqs.question: The proton‑motive force that drives ATP synthesis consists of which two components?
options: Electrical potential (Δψ) and chemical concentration gradient (ΔpH)
mcqs.explanation: Proton‑motive force (Δp) = Δψ (membrane potential) + (2.303RT/F)·ΔpH, representing both electrical and chemical components of the gradient.

mcqs.question: Which inhibitor specifically blocks ATP synthesis by preventing proton flow through ATP synthase?
mcqs.explanation: Oligomycin binds to the F₀ subunit of ATP synthase, halting proton translocation and thus stopping ATP formation.

mcqs.question: During chemiosmosis, the re‑entry of protons into the mitochondrial matrix through ATP synthase is directly coupled to
mcqs.explanation: The energy released by protons moving down their gradient drives the catalytic activity of ATP synthase, converting ADP + Pi into ATP.

mcqs.question: ATP synthase is embedded in which mitochondrial membrane?
mcqs.explanation: ATP synthase resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane where the proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain is utilized for ATP synthesis.

mcqs.question: The F1 sector of ATP synthase protrudes into which mitochondrial compartment?
mcqs.explanation: The soluble F1 catalytic domain extends into the mitochondrial matrix, where ADP and inorganic phosphate bind for phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: During oxidative phosphorylation, the flow of protons through ATP synthase drives rotation of which subunit?
mcqs.explanation: Proton translocation through the F0 channel causes rotation of the central gamma shaft, inducing conformational changes in the three beta subunits that synthesize ATP.

mcqs.question: Approximately how many protons must pass through one ATP synthase complex to synthesize one molecule of ATP (including ADP and Pi transport) in mitochondria?
mcqs.explanation: About four protons are required per ATP: three drive the rotary mechanism and one is used by the phosphate transporter (Pi/H+ symporter).

mcqs.question: Which antibiotic specifically inhibits the F0 portion of mitochondrial ATP synthase, blocking proton translocation?
mcqs.explanation: Oligomycin binds to the F0 channel, preventing proton flow and thereby halting ATP synthesis.

mcqs.question: If the mitochondrial membrane potential collapses, ATP synthase can operate in reverse. What is the net result?
options: ATP hydrolysis to pump protons back into the intermembrane space
ATP synthesis without a proton gradient
Generation of heat without ATP turnover
mcqs.explanation: In reverse mode, ATP synthase hydrolyzes ATP to pump protons against the gradient, helping to re‑establish the membrane potential.

mcqs.question: In chloroplasts, the enzyme analogous to mitochondrial ATP synthase is called:
mcqs.explanation: Chloroplasts contain a similar rotary enzyme named CF1CF0‑ATP synthase (also called chloroplast ATP synthase) that uses the light‑driven proton gradient to make ATP.

mcqs.question: Which of the following complexes of the mitochondrial electron transport chain does NOT pump protons across the inner membrane?
mcqs.explanation: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons from FADH2 to ubiquinone but does not translocate protons, unlike Complexes I, III and IV.

mcqs.question: What is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: Molecular oxygen accepts electrons at Complex IV, being reduced to water, which is the terminal step of the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: According to the chemiosmotic theory, ATP synthesis during oxidative phosphorylation is driven by:
options: Proton flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase
mcqs.explanation: The return of protons from the intermembrane space to the matrix through the F0‑F1 ATP synthase provides the energy for phosphorylation of ADP to ATP.

mcqs.question: Approximately how many ATP molecules are synthesized per NADH oxidized (P/O ratio) in oxidative phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: Each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP molecules because electrons pass through Complexes I, III and IV, pumping enough protons to generate roughly 2.5 ATP per NADH.

mcqs.question: Which inhibitor specifically blocks electron transfer from cytochrome b to cytochrome c in the electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: Antimycin A binds to Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex) and prevents the transfer of electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, halting proton pumping at this step.

mcqs.question: The proton motive force that drives ATP synthesis consists of which two components?
mcqs.explanation: The proton motive force is the sum of the membrane electrical potential (Δψ) and the transmembrane pH gradient (ΔpH) generated by electron transport.

mcqs.question: On which side of the inner mitochondrial membrane does the catalytic domain of ATP synthase synthesize ATP?
options: Intermembrane space side of inner membrane
mcqs.explanation: ATP synthase releases newly formed ATP into the mitochondrial matrix, where the catalytic β‑subunits are located.

mcqs.question: Which molecule acts as the final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain of aerobic respiration?
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen has the highest reduction potential among common biological electron acceptors, allowing it to receive electrons at the end of the chain and be reduced to water.

mcqs.question: In the electron transport chain, reduction of the terminal electron acceptor leads to the formation of which compound?
mcqs.explanation: When O₂ accepts electrons and combines with protons at Complex IV, it is reduced to H₂O, completing the chain.

mcqs.question: What is the immediate consequence of a deficiency of the terminal electron acceptor during cellular respiration?
options: The electron transport chain halts, decreasing ATP synthesis
mcqs.explanation: Without O₂ to accept electrons, the chain backs up, NADH and FADH₂ cannot be oxidized, and oxidative phosphorylation stops, leading to reduced ATP production.

mcqs.question: In certain anaerobic microorganisms, nitrate (NO₃⁻) can serve as an alternative terminal electron acceptor. What is the primary reduced product formed?
mcqs.explanation: Nitrate is first reduced to nitrite during anaerobic respiration; further reductions may produce other nitrogen species, but nitrite is the immediate product.

mcqs.question: Why is oxygen considered a more efficient terminal electron acceptor than many other potential acceptors?
options: It has a very high reduction potential, releasing large free‑energy change
It is abundant in the cytosol
It can donate electrons directly to NADH
It does not require a membrane potential
mcqs.explanation: The high reduction potential of O₂ (≈+0.82 V) provides a large ΔG⁰′ when electrons flow to it, driving substantial proton pumping and ATP synthesis.

mcqs.question: Transfer of electrons to the terminal electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation is coupled with which process?
options: Proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Direct synthesis of ATP by substrate‑level phosphorylation
mcqs.explanation: Complexes I, III, and IV use the energy from electron transfer to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating the electrochemical gradient used by ATP synthase.

mcqs.question: Which mitochondrial complex directly transfers electrons to the terminal electron acceptor?
mcqs.explanation: Complex IV receives electrons from cytochrome c and transfers them to O₂, reducing it to water.

mcqs.question: Which of the following reactions correctly represents the reduction of oxygen to water in the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
mcqs.explanation: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers four electrons to one O2 molecule and combines them with four protons from the matrix to produce two molecules of H2O.

mcqs.question: How many molecules of water are produced when a single NADH molecule is oxidized completely in oxidative phosphorylation?
mcqs.explanation: Two electrons from one NADH reduce half an O2 molecule, yielding one H2O molecule per NADH.

mcqs.question: Which inner‑mitochondrial‑membrane complex directly reduces oxygen to water?
mcqs.explanation: Complex IV receives electrons from cytochrome c and reduces O2 to H2O, completing the electron transport chain.

mcqs.question: In the overall balanced equation for aerobic respiration of glucose, how many water molecules are formed as products?
mcqs.explanation: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O; thus six molecules of water are generated.

mcqs.question: Where does the actual formation of water occur during oxidative phosphorylation?
options: In the mitochondrial matrix by ATP synthase
On the intermembrane side of Complex I
On the matrix side of Complex IV
On the intermembrane side of Complex III
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen is reduced to water at Complex IV on the matrix side of the inner membrane, where protons are released back into the matrix.

mcqs.question: What is the role of molecular oxygen in water formation during the electron transport chain?
options: It acts as an electron donor
It is the final electron acceptor that combines with protons to form water
It serves as a substrate for ATP synthase
It functions as a catalyst for NADH oxidation
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and, together with protons, is reduced to H2O, completing oxidative phosphorylation.

mcqs.question: Respiratory quotient (RQ) is defined as:
options: Ratio of O2 consumed to CO2 produced
Ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed
Ratio of ATP produced to O2 consumed
Ratio of glucose consumed to O2 produced
mcqs.explanation: RQ is the ratio of the volume (or moles) of CO2 generated to the volume (or moles) of O2 utilized during metabolism.

mcqs.question: The typical respiratory quotient for pure carbohydrate oxidation is:
mcqs.explanation: Oxidation of carbohydrates yields equal moles of CO2 and O2, giving an RQ of about 1.0.

mcqs.question: An RQ value of 0.75 most likely indicates predominant oxidation of:
mcqs.explanation: Fat oxidation produces less CO2 per O2 consumed, giving an RQ around 0.7–0.75, lower than that for carbs or proteins.

mcqs.question: Complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose (C6H12O6) yields how many moles of CO2 and O2 respectively, and what is the resulting RQ?
mcqs.explanation: One glucose molecule produces 6 CO2 and consumes 6 O2, so RQ = 6/6 = 1.0.

mcqs.question: During prolonged fasting, the respiratory quotient typically falls to around 0.7 because:
mcqs.explanation: Fasting shifts metabolism toward fat oxidation, which yields a lower CO2/O2 ratio, giving an RQ near 0.7.
